items.title: Roscoe Mitchell interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 23, 2023
items.q: But I go way back with Karl Berger... So I used to hang out with him and go down there and there would always be these sessions and so on and so forth.

ctx.x: Very interesting. It makes me think a little bit about a quote I had a conversation with Karl Berger, the late Karl Berger. And he said — we were talking about sort of free jazz, and he said, “More freedom is not about less precision it’s about more precision. The more precise you get the more free you are. People think of a sense of freedom, free jazz, oh I can lose all the rules. I’m actually creating my own rules and they’re much more stringent.”

Absolutely. He’s totally right on that. You know. Totally right. But I go way back with Karl Berger. When I was in the Army in Heidelberg, Germany, there was a K-54 and Karl Berger was down there with the musicians down there — Albert Mangelsdorff was there, Bent Jaedig, the great tenor saxophonist from Denmark, and you know Nathaniel Davis, his quartet had won the All-Army championship or whatever, so they came to live with us in Heidelberg. So I used to hang out with him and go down there and there would always…

All right. I want to take you back a little bit before that and I read that in 1961 you had what this review said, a hard bop group and Joseph Jarman and Anthony Braxton. My question is at that point, in 1961, Coltrane released “My Favorite Things” and Ornette Coleman “Free Jazz,” Max Roach had a “Freedom Suite,” and one of my favorites, Hank Mobley had an LP called “Roll Call.” Was there decision-making for you at that point in your career about your direction? © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
